summary: VEX-Bench: 75 expert-labelled cases (67 CVEs, 35 projects; 25 Java, 30 Go, 20 Python) in which an agent receives a full downstream repository snapshot plus a known CVE in a dependency and must decide whether the project is affected and, if not, why (four VEX-style justifications). Nine models are evaluated in vendor or open harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) over three runs and compared with OSV-Scanner, Trivy and govulncheck.

claims.claim: Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5 reach ~80% F1 on binary affected/not-affected classification.
claims.evidence: Table 2: status F1 81.6 +/- 3.8 (Opus 4.6, Claude Code) and 79.9 +/- 8.0 (GPT-5.5, Codex); accuracy 88.4 / 89.3. Matches abstract. Note only 29.3% of cases are affected (Fig. 2), so an always-'not affected' predictor gets ~70.7% accuracy; MiniMax-M2.7 (71.1%) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (72.9%) are near that floor.

claims.claim: Only GPT-5.5 exceeds 70% macro-F1 on fine-grained justification; justification is harder than status for every configuration.
claims.evidence: Table 2: GPT-5.5 justification macro-F1 73.5 +/- 3.3, next best Kimi K2.6 64.6 +/- 7.9; justification accuracy < status accuracy for all nine (largest gap GPT-5.4 mini 15.5 pp). Some justification classes have very few cases (Limitations), so macro-F1 is noisy.

claims.claim: Traditional SCA tools cannot reliably distinguish affected projects from false alerts.
claims.evidence: Table 3: OSV-Scanner F1 40.5, Trivy 36.1 (precision 27.4 / 26.0) on n=75; Go-only OSV reachability F1 42.9, govulncheck 25.0 (completes 19/30). Mapping rule 'affected iff tool reports the CVE' on cases selected because the manifest was patched for that CVE makes high recall / low precision nearly guaranteed.

claims.claim: Harness choice affects inference cost far more than classification performance.
claims.evidence: Fig. 7: only two models (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 mini) under two harnesses (Codex CLI vs OpenCode); Codex better for GPT-5.5 at >2x tokens, comparable for mini at ~4x tokens. Main table confounds harness with model family (vendor harness for closed models, OpenCode for open weights).

claims.claim: No meaningful model-side leakage from source PRs.
claims.evidence: Appendix C: manual audit of all 75 source PRs (3 discuss exploitability, none state the label); guided-completion probe on 19 PRs: GPT-5.5 1 exact match of 19, Opus 4.6 0 of 19. Agents had web access during evaluation (§3.4).

patterns.note: Task requires reasoning across an upstream advisory and a downstream repo (dependency call sites); benchmark measures this but proposes no coordination mechanism.
New agent benchmark with 3-run means/SD, Docker isolation, git-history stripping and leakage probe.
All runs in isolated Docker containers separated from labels and evaluation artifacts to prevent benchmark hacking.
Reports per-case tokens and dollar cost; Pareto analysis shows DeepSeek-V4-Pro ($0.075) and GLM-5.1 ($0.095) near frontier vs GPT-5.5 ($1.082).
Cost-performance data (Fig. 3) could inform cheap-model routing for triage, but routing is not evaluated.
Compares agents against static SCA tools (OSV-Scanner, Trivy, govulncheck) that are the usual deterministic baseline.

methodology.sample: 75 cases from PRs in top-100 starred permissive repos referencing a CVE and modifying a manifest/lockfile; 22 affected vs 53 not affected (29.3% / 70.7%).
methodology.baselines: OSV-Scanner, Trivy (full), OSV reachability and govulncheck (Go only); no majority-class or simple LLM-without-agent baseline.
methodology.models: Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Claude Code); GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 mini (Codex); Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, MiniMax-M2.7, GLM-5.1 (OpenCode).
methodology.variance: Mean +/- SD over three runs per configuration; SDs up to ~13 pp on recall/F1.
methodology.ablations: Harness ablation for two GPT models only; language and repo-size breakdowns for four configurations.
methodology.contamination_controls: Labels never public; Docker isolation; git history removed; manual PR audit and guided-completion memorization probe (Appendix C).
methodology.languages: Java (25 cases, median 546K LOC), Go (30), Python (20); no JavaScript/npm.

standards.artifacts: Code and data at github.com/steven1518/vex-bench; full prompt and label-mapping in Appendix B; environment details Appendix D.

biases.detail: 75 cases, 22 affected; some justification classes have only a handful of cases, making macro-F1 and per-language splits fragile.
Closed models run only in their vendor harness and open models only in OpenCode, so model and harness effects are entangled in Table 2.
No majority-class baseline reported despite 70.7% not-affected prior; status accuracy near 71-73% for weaker models is close to trivial.

SCA tools are scored 'affected iff CVE reported' on cases selected because the CVE triggered a manifest change, so low precision is partly by construction; still a realistic description of how these tools are used.
Gold justification uses a precedence rule; §4.4.3 shows 4 of 5 reviewed GPT-5.5 'errors' were defensible alternative labels.

verdict_reason: Carefully built, released, peer-reviewed benchmark with multi-run variance and leakage checks, and headline numbers match Table 2; but n=75 with heavy class imbalance and no majority baseline, harness-model confounding, and a two-model harness ablation limit the stronger conclusions.
applicability: Directly useful for the Java team's dependency hygiene across several repositories: Java is the largest subset (25 cases, median 546K LOC, Maven/Gradle manifests), and the results suggest an agent triage step on top of Dependabot/OSV/Trivy alerts can cut false positives (SCA precision ~26-27% vs agents ~75-89%), with cheaper open models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GLM-5.1) near the cost-performance frontier. For mixed agent hosts, the harness ablation hints that host choice mainly changes token cost, but that evidence is thin (two models). Treat agent output as a VEX justification proposal that a human or deterministic reachability check confirms, given ~20-30% justification error; nothing here touches domain content or spec-driven development.

conflicts_with.detail: Claw-SWE-Bench reports that harness choice changes success rate substantially with the model fixed, whereas VEX-Bench's (two-model) ablation concludes harness affects cost far more than performance.
